item.title: POINT OF ORIGIN | A life built on faith and perseverance
item.description: KEOLA Pati’s life has been shaped by work, family, faith and perseverance. From her early working days, when she travelled by speedboat to island resorts to sewing curtains, to raising a family through difficult times and working for decades in Fiji’s furniture and retail industries, she learned to keep going regardless of the circumstances. She faced fear, financial hardship, loss and uncertainty
item.content:encoded:
KEOLA Pati’s life has been shaped by work, family, faith and perseverance. From her early working days, when she travelled by speedboat to island resorts to sewing curtains, to raising a family through difficult times and working for decades in Fiji’s furniture and retail industries, she learned to keep going regardless of the circumstances.

She faced fear, financial hardship, loss and uncertainty, but also experienced the kindness of workmates and people who helped her along the way.

Now, 86, and still working, Keola’s story offers a glimpse into a generation shaped by discipline, responsibility and the belief that when there is work to be done, you simply do it.

For a young Keola Pati, the water rushing past was frightening. She watched the boat cut across the sea, carrying her towards an unfamiliar island and a job she had agreed to take.

She was going to work on an island in the Mamanuca Group.

That moment, many decades ago, would become one of countless moments in Keola’s life when fear could have stopped her — but did not.

Today, she can look back on a life defined not by the absence of hardship, but by her determination to keep going through it.

For Keola, the foundation of her life was laid in childhood.

Her parents were her first teachers, teaching her the responsibilities and expectations that shaped the woman she would become.

“The first teacher used to be our parents.”

At home, there was little room for questioning.

“They teach us, you do this, you do that, you do that.”

You woke up, did what needed to be done and carried on.

When Keola began working, those childhood lessons became reality.

“When I start to work, I wake up in the morning, I go to work, do the job then come back home, then do the cooking, washing, everything.”

There was always something to do but hardship also taught her endurance.

When she first started working at Hensher (Fiji) Ltd, – a UK-based household manufacturing company that operated in Fiji during the 1970s and 1980s – her boss asked if she could go to the Reef Hotel for work.

The materials and machines were loaded onto a boat and Keola went with them.

Her job was to measure and sew curtains.

It was the beginning of a working life that would take her to different islands, including Mana Island and Castaway Island.

For a young woman travelling alone for work, it was an experience filled with unfamiliar surroundings and moments of fear.

The first speedboat journey remains vivid in her memory.

Working away from home brought other challenges.

One night, while staying on an island, Keola saw a snake near her door.

“I was so frightened. I can’t yell, I can’t do anything. I just pray to God, ‘please God, you help me’.”

For Keola, the experience reinforced something she had learned from her parents — faith. Prayer became a constant part of her life.

It travelled with her wherever work took her.

“Only prayer can change things. Nothing else.

“Anything you want to do, first you pray to God. You must pray when the sun rise.”

Her faith became a source of strength during the difficult years that followed.

item.title: FOCUS I Setting its sights on renewal
item.description: THE Methodist Church in Fiji is preparing to enter a new chapter of self-examination and renewal, with its ministers being challenged to confront the personal burdens that can limit their leadership and service. The challenge came from the church’s outgoing president, Reverend Dr. Semisi Turagavou, during his address to the Ministerial Session of the 2026 Annual Conference in Suva, where he announ
item.content:encoded:
THE Methodist Church in Fiji is preparing to enter a new chapter of self-examination and renewal, with its ministers being challenged to confront the personal burdens that can limit their leadership and service.

The challenge came from the church’s outgoing president, Reverend Dr. Semisi Turagavou, during his address to the Ministerial Session of the 2026 Annual Conference in Suva, where he announced that 2027–2028 would be observed across the Connexion as the “Year of Liberation and Reformation.”

The theme he said, follows directly from the previous Conference theme, “Elevating Christ’s Church to Another Level,” which called on the church to deepen its spiritual life, integrity and effectiveness.

But Mr Turagavou acknowledged that the call to elevation had not been fully realised.

While there had been signs of growth and renewed commitment in many congregations, he told ministers that elevation “was not achieved everywhere” and that some continued to carry burdens, many of them self-imposed that had held them back.

“A church cannot be elevated while her ministers remain shackled. You cannot lift a people while carrying chains yourself,” he told delegates.

For Mr Turagavou, the new conference theme is not simply a slogan for the wider Church. It begins with the people entrusted to lead it.

Drawing on the biblical account of Israel’s liberation at Sinai and Christ’s proclamation of liberty in Luke 4, he said liberation must come before reformation.

That process, he stressed must begin within the ministry before it can extend to congregations.

The centre of his address was therefore a direct appeal for greater personal discipline among ordained ministers and lay pastors.

One of the most candid issues he raised was the excessive consumption of yaqona within the ministry.

He made clear that his concern was not with the culture itself, but with self-discipline and the consequences of over-consumption.

He said excessive consumption had, in some cases, contributed to reduced pastoral visitation, weaker sermon preparation and Bible study, lower attendance at training program and diminished energy for evangelism and outreach.

The consequences, he said extended beyond individual ministers to their wellbeing and the public witness of the church.

He also reaffirmed the church’s existing discipline on smoking and called for the same standard to apply with equal seriousness to lay pastors and ordained ministers.

Congregations, he noted do not distinguish between the two when judging the example set by those who lead them.

Financial pressure was another area Mr Turagavou placed before ministers as part of the call to liberation.

He urged ministers to confront financial bondage arising from loans, credit purchases and unnecessary borrowing.

The process of becoming “unshackled”, he said, should be disciplined and prayerful.

He also encouraged ministers to prepare early for retirement rather than leaving such planning until later in their careers.

Among his suggestions were acquiring land and building a home during the years of active service.

He also encouraged voluntary membership of the Fiji National Provident Fund as one way of preparing for a dignified retirement.

The financial message to ministers came as the annual conference also received a report showing that the Methodist Church in Fiji remains in a strong overall financial position.

According to the church, as of May 31, 2025, the Church’s total assets had increased from $55.51 million in 2024 to $58.63 million in 2025, an increase of about $3.12 million.

Liabilities rose only marginally, from $4.52 million to $4.58 million, while net assets increased from $50.99 million to $54.05 million.

A major contributor was the growth in financial assets, particularly equity investments, which increased from about $37.95 million to $42.22 million.

Property, plant and equipment also increased, from $8.42 million to $8.69 million.

The report showed accumulated funds of $23.27 million and an unrealised gains reserve of $30.79 million.

However, the church’s cash and cash equivalents declined from about $7.70 million in 2024 to $5.64 million in 2025, highlighting the importance of continued attention to cash flow and liquidity management.

Character, health and the example of leadership

item.title: EXPERIENCE I From darkness to devotion
item.description: At 4.30 every morning, while much of the country is still asleep, Seva Manjari Devi Dasi is already awake. The temple is stirring. Worship is about to begin, and she rises to take her place among the devotees at the Sri Radha Damodar Temple in Sigatoka.
item.content:encoded:
At 4.30 every morning, while much of the country is still asleep, Seva Manjari Devi Dasi is already awake.

The temple is stirring. Worship is about to begin, and she rises to take her place among the devotees at the Sri Radha Damodar Temple in Sigatoka.

For the 25-year-old iTaukei woman, this quiet routine represents more than a change in where she lives. It marks a profound departure from the life she once knew.

Born Vaseva Rokotiko, she was raised in an orphanage in Nadi before being adopted. She grew up in a humble environment, later attended school in Nadi and eventually worked at Hilton Fiji on Denarau Island.

Today, she has a new name, a new faith and, in her words, “a new life”.

“I come from an Assemblies of God background, and I find the Hare Krishna movement a very peaceful space. It’s stress-free. That’s one of the greatest things that I feel about this place, just peace and harmony.”

Rokotiko, originally from Kavula in Bua, Vanua Levu, says she never knew her father. Her mother eventually adopted her, but before that she spent part of her childhood at Treasure Home in Nadi.

She attended A.D. Patel Memorial Primary School from Class 1 to 8 before completing Forms 3 to 7 at Ratu Navula College. She left school in 2019 as a vocational student.

Her working life took her into hospitality, but it was caring for elderly people that eventually gave her a deeper sense of purpose.

In 2025, she accepted a job caring for a 79-year-old Indo-Fijian woman in Simla, Lautoka. The woman had suffered a stroke and was bedridden. She was also a Hare Krishna devotee.

Rokotiko’s responsibilities were intimate and demanding: feeding her, bathing her and attending to her personal needs.

Rokotiko then moved to Votualevu in Nadi, where she cared for another elderly patient for three months.

“As you can see, I love looking after elderly people. That is my passion.”

She believes that affection for elderly people was rooted in her childhood and the time she spent with her grandparents.

“I guess it’s because of my upbringing, I used to enjoy being around my grandparents, and that’s when I started to develop my liking for looking after old people.”

Her connection with Hare Krishna, however, began before she ever imagined becoming a devotee.

While living with a brother in Narere, Nasinu, her neighbours were Hare Krishna devotees. She would hear their chanting and songs and gradually became curious about the faith.

She remembers being drawn not initially by doctrine, but by the sound of music and singing.

“I would listen to their songs, and I started to admire the way they sang and started following the tune of the songs.”

Then, in February this year, another opportunity brought her to the Sri Radha Damodar Temple in Sigatoka, this time to care for an elderly woman there.

What began as a job slowly became something much larger.

Her days at the temple are structured around service.

There is worship at 4.30am, another at 6am and the final worship of the day at 6.30pm. In between, she works wherever she is needed.

Some days she is in the kitchen. Other days she sweeps the steps, works at reception, cares for the elderly or participates in worship.

“My experience looking after the elderly, especially the vulnerable ones who are not able to help themselves, has been very enriching journey. It’s a very good experience. I like the idea of serving the sick and vulnerable.”

That philosophy of service has become central to her understanding of her new faith.

“At the temple, you are far removed from the stresses of life and the desire to seek out luxury and things of this world, and you are just focused on serving God and serving humanity. To me, that is a very, very noble calling.”

Recently, her commitment took another step when she was initiated into the Hare Krishna movement.

She is no longer simply Vaseva Rokotiko.

“My new name is Seva Manjari Devi Dasi,” she proudly says.

item.title: WOMEN’S HEALTH I No woman should face birth alone
item.description: THE first sign that Deborah Strong was in trouble was not the two bottles of breast milk sitting beside her more than two decades ago. She was still wearing the previous day’s clothes. Her hair had not been brushed. She had been awake, feeding and expressing milk, until the days and nights had begun to blur into one long stretch of motherhood.
item.content:encoded:
THE first sign that Deborah Strong was in trouble was not the two bottles of breast milk sitting beside her more than two decades ago.

She was still wearing the previous day’s clothes. Her hair had not been brushed. She had been awake, feeding and expressing milk, until the days and nights had begun to blur into one long stretch of motherhood.

Her mother, Caroline, had come to check on her. She took one look at her daughter and said: “Deb this is not sustainable. You can’t continue like this.”

Strong had been home two weeks with her first baby, Ella. She had read everything she could about breastfeeding during pregnancy and thought she was prepared.

But motherhood had presented her with a problem no book had been able to solve. Her daughter had been given a bottle at hospital, and immediately afterwards struggled to return to the breast. Strong had plenty of milk, but her baby could not settle into breastfeeding.

The routine was exhausting. She would offer the breast, try again, eventually give the baby expressed milk in a bottle, settle her, then wait for her to sleep so she could pump again. By the time she finished, the baby was almost ready to wake.

“You become sleep-deprived very very quickly in a more urgent way,” she recalls

For two weeks, Strong kept going. Her mother noticed what she had failed to notice herself: she was exhausted.

As luck would have it, there was a woman who had recently arrived in Fiji, specialised in breastfeeding support. Strong’s mum recommended the lady – Carolyn Tranter, the founder of Doula Beginnings and Ocean’s only DONA International-arpproved doula trainer.

Tranter eventually visited. Rather than taking over, she watched.

“Carry on as if I’m not here. I’m going to just observe and see what could be, and what and where we could improve things but you do what you are doing and then I’ll know what to do,” she told me.

“I had read about different breastfeeding positions and tried them all. Cradle, cross-cradle, side-lying, football and reclining. Nothing seemed to work.”

But the woman watching could see what the new mum could not. Strong had established breastfeeding, and her milk was flowing quickly. Her baby was struggling with the speed of it.

It was a small but important lesson. For three days they worked together until Strong’s daughter was breastfeeding normally again.

The bottles and breast pump no longer dictated the routine. Strong was feeding her daughter herself, every two hours, and sleeping more. She had regained something almost as important as the ability to breastfeed: confidence. And then she asked the woman who had helped her to teach her what she knew.

“I told Carolyn, whatever this is can you please show me because I am so lucky you stopped at my mum’s office. There are people in my country who need this service and I would I’d love to learn it so I can help as many women as I can.”

That request, made in the aftermath of her own difficult start to motherhood, set Strong on a path she has followed for 26 years.

Strong’s journey into doula work did not begin with a business plan.

It began with gratitude. She understood that not every woman had what she had. She had her mother. She had family and a community around her. But what about the woman who had none of those things?

Strong remembers asking herself what happened to women who were going from house to house, had no family support, no income and no money for alternatives when breastfeeding (and both prenatal and post-nala care) became difficult.

She began training with Carolyn Tranter, accompanying her to clients, observing her work and learning along the way.

Her first experience as a trainee came close to home when she helped support her own sister during pregnancy and the birth of her nephew.

It was the beginning of a role that would become a lifetime commitment.

The word doula is still unfamiliar to many people in Fiji.

Strong describes it simply as: “A doula is a woman in service to women in labour.”

“The doula is not there to control the birth but to provide support.

“Birth can change direction quickly. Medical intervention may become necessary. A woman’s carefully imagined birth may not happen the way she hoped.”

But even when circumstances change, she should not feel powerless.

“The doula helps a woman understand what is happening and supports her as she makes her way through it.”

For Strong, doula care begins well before labour.

item.title: DISCOVERING FIJI I From a Pacific voyage to a legacy learning
item.description: THE story of Fulton Adventist University did not begin with a classroom. It began with the sea. On August 3, 1891, the ship Pitcairn arrived in Fiji on its maiden voyage across the Pacific. Among those aboard were John I. Tay and his wife, the first Seventh-day Adventists to set foot on Fijian soil.
item.content:encoded:
THE story of Fulton Adventist University did not begin with a classroom. It began with the sea.

On August 3, 1891, the ship Pitcairn arrived in Fiji on its maiden voyage across the Pacific. Among those aboard were John I. Tay and his wife, the first Seventh-day Adventists to set foot on Fijian soil.

They came at a time when the Pacific was still a vast chain of islands separated by thousands of miles of ocean, yet connected by a growing conviction that the Christian message should reach every shore.

Tay and his wife remained in Fiji after the Pitcairn continued its journey. But their story would take a sorrowful turn.

Six months later, Tay fell ill and died. He was buried in Suva, far from the places he had known and among people whose land, language and way of life were still vastly strange.

The mission did not end at his grave. By July 1895, the Adventist work in Fiji had begun again. John and Fanny Cole arrived from Norfolk Island, followed by John and Susie Fulton from New Zealand and, later, Calvin and Myrtle Parker.

The early missionaries faced the familiar realities of life in early Fiji – distance, unfamiliar languages and cultures, travel between islands and villages, and the enormous task of establishing a church in a place where people were mostly pagan.

But among them was a man who saw that the future could not depend forever on missionaries arriving from overseas.

He was John Fulton was an educator at heart.

He believed that teaching indigenous workers was an essential part of mission work and one of the greatest contributions expatriate missionaries could make to the Church. The message, he understood, would have its deepest roots when Fijians themselves were trained to teach, preach and lead.

That conviction would eventually change the course of Adventist education in Fiji.

At first, the plan was to send Fijian workers to Avondale College in Australia. It seemed a sensible solution. The Church already had an established institution where students could receive training.

But between Fiji and Australia lay the expansive Pacific Ocean.

For Fijian students, travelling overseas was not a simple matter. There were the difficulties of leaving home, the cost and logistics of travel, and the English-language competency required by Australian authorities for student visas.

At this point, the Church was faced with a practical question. If Fijian workers could not easily be sent across the sea for training, why not establish the training here?

The answer came in November 1903 when the first Fijian Church Council decided to develop the Fiji Training Institute, the foreunner of today’s Fulton Adventist University.

The Adventist Church in Fiji was still small—about 150 members in only four churches. Yet those few believers were looking beyond their own numbers. They were thinking about the generations who would follow them.

Fulton College would eventually trace its roots to that momentous decision.

The Fiji Training Institute was commissioned in 1903 under the leadership of John Fulton, superintendent of the Fiji Mission. It was the beginning of an educational journey that would take the institution through several names, several locations and many seasons of change.

But the purpose remained -train people for service.

The first task was to find a suitable home.

Suvavou, where the Adventist Church had first established itself, was considered unsuitable for a training institute. So the leaders began searching, praying and looking for a place where a school could grow.

Their search led them across the sea to Ovalau.

At Buresala they found 276 acres of land, a property blessed with rich soil, water and timber. It was about 11 miles overland, or 16 miles by water, from Levuka, then the capital of Fiji.

Buresala offered space for a school, a farm, a printing operation and a growing mission community. In the thinking of those early leaders, education and practical work belonged together. Students could learn with their hands as well as their minds, while the land could help sustain the institution.

The Church also planned to move its headquarters from Suvavou to Buresala.

In 1905, Fulton’s house at Suvavou was dismantled.

Piece by piece, it was taken apart and transported by sea to the new site. There, it was put together again and converted into a duplex. One side became the home of John Fulton, superintendent of the mission. The other was occupied by Carr, principal of the new Fiji Training Institute.

One was used for the printing press. Another was for supplies. Six were provided for students. It was not a grand campus by modern standards.

But for those who gathered there, it represented something much bigger.

item.title: REFLECTION I Decision of destiny
item.description: This poem is inspired by life and the choices that people make in life. I was a secondary school student in Fiji when I read a short sentence written on the back of a door, in a restaurant.
item.content:encoded:
This poem is inspired by life and the choices that people make in life.

I was a secondary school student in Fiji when I read a short sentence written on the back of a door, in a restaurant.

The sentence was profound: ‘Decision determines destiny’

No matter what the circumstances in life may be. No matter the karma we arrived with at birth. No matter the choices we choose upon our journey. All persons were also born with free will.

Free will is the belief that people have an opportunity/ability to choose and control their course of action – and also their reaction – to situations, as per their moral responsibility and response. The premise of free will is that people are at liberty to make an independent choice and moral responsibility is the attribution of approval or disapproval, based upon their choice(s).

It is said that the dawn is always invincible. No matter the choices that people made yesterday, with the morn, a new day is born, as an opportunity for people to change their path.

Sometimes, one’s life path is hindered by circumstances of birth, the ill-intentions of other people upon their path, the karma of their previous lives and similar factors.

Nonetheless, until one’s day is done, people must keep sailing on. Sometimes, their journey is blessed and sometimes their faith is tested to see if they have the endurance to face the eye of the storm. This is an exercise in self-awareness and self-acceptance.

During my childhood days, my father repeated one message to me – ‘No matter what other people do, you walk upon your path with purpose. They may seek to lure you with distractions but your duty and dedication is your life legacy.’

Just as a bird is dependent on her wings and not on the tree branch to support her, so people who are as self-reliant as is possible; who strive for a life of purpose; who are not dependent upon a tree branch that has the probability to break away, have placed themselves in a situation to live a fulfilling life.

Some people select detachment and withdraw from society. Some people choose the attachment approach and seek to guide others on their life path. Blessed be their empathy for others and blessed be those who choose to listen and learn.

Of course, there are many paths to learning in life:

– some seek the grace of guidance from other persons

– some learn through love – whether tender or tough

In all circumstances, people have the free will to choose their actions and reactions. They can bow to pressure or to purpose.

This poem was initially inspired by a special soul who made an error in life and was paraded by his State throughout his court trial without restraint, owing to his vulnerability at that moment in time.

He remains incarcerated to this day in a correction facility and there, he found his purpose in life. He matured enough to release himself of previous errors in character. He discovered spirituality and became an assistant to his Sunday School teacher. Soon, he was assigned an additional role – he was promoted to the rank of teacher and permitted to teach his colleagues in the correction facility, basic school curriculum subjects.

As the years passed by, he chose to accept full responsibility for the events that led to his incarceration, although it was a sequence of events that was the true cause of the tragic accident.

Despite numerous attempts for his release, it has not been granted by the State and so he continues to be the sunflower soul that he is. Always walking in the light and guiding others towards the light, with him.

The fact that he chose to transform his life despite his circumstances is a lesson for those that seek change. He is likely due for an early release but for now – and of his own observation – he stands on the outside and watches the ways of the world.

Our existence on earth is one moment in time.

Whatever path we choose to walk upon – our decision determines our destiny.

In all circumstances, people have the free will to choose their actions and reactions. They can bow to pressure or to purpose. Picture: SUPPLIED

item.title: FEATURE I Building champions, shaping lives
item.description: SOLO Baleisolomone’s story isn’t just about rugby; it’s about building a legacy from humble beginnings. By trade, Solo is a construction site manager in the UK.
item.content:encoded:
SOLO Baleisolomone’s story isn’t just about rugby; it’s about building a legacy from humble beginnings.

By trade, Solo is a construction site manager in the UK.

Day in, day out, he builds structures, solves problems, and takes responsibility for getting things done the right way. But beyond the hard hats and site plans, there’s a deeper calling that drives him, one rooted in family, culture, and giving others a chance.

With no funding, no shortcuts, and no guarantees, Solo founded Kaiviti Rugby Academy (KRA) UK. It started with a vision of creating opportunities for young players, especially those connected to Fijian rugby culture, to be seen, developed, and believed in. What he built wasn’t just an academy. It became a home. A place where discipline is taught, identity is embraced, and potential is unlocked.

And that vision quickly turned into action on the big stage. KRA 7s stepped into the highly competitive London International Tournament 7s Series, one of the toughest 7s circuits in the UK, and completed all three tournaments in the series.

From starting with nothing to competing across multiple elite events, it was a statement of intent. The results weren’t just about wins or losses; it was proof that KRA belongs, that the pathway is real, and that something powerful is being built.

In one of the most powerful chapters of his journey, he took in eight young Fijian girls, welcoming them into his own home, providing not just coaching, but accommodation, support, and a family environment.

Under the Lilian Rugby team, he developed them, believed in them, and gave them a platform many never thought possible.

He then led them into the same elite arena: The London international tournament 7s series, where they competed with pride, passion, and purpose. And then came history.

At Harpenden 7s, that same group went on to win, becoming the first Fijian women’s team to win a UK Women’s Elite 7s tournament. It wasn’t just a victory on the field. It was a moment that represented sacrifice, belief, and opportunity coming together. A group that started with a dream, guided by one man’s vision, stood at the top and made history.

But the real story of Solo isn’t just in the teams he’s built; it’s in the lives he’s shaped, starting with his own children.

His daughter, Lukcyana, lived his legacy. From the early days of being coached by her father, learning the game step by step, she has grown into a high-level athlete now playing with Oaklands College under the Saracens Girls Academy. She has also earned her place in the England U18 girls player development group, and has already stepped into an England camp, an incredible milestone, with her journey still only just beginning. That progression didn’t happen by chance. It was built, through sacrifice, consistency, belief, and a father who refused to let limits define what was possible.

Alongside her, Solo’s son, Tui, is carving his own path.

A proud competitor, Tui stepped into adult rugby with Shelford RFC’s 1st team, showing resilience after time away from the game and making his mark in his first full season. His journey, like his sister’s, reflects the same values their father lives by: sheer determination, pride, and perseverance.

For Solo, this is what it’s all about. It’s about showing his children and every player he coaches that where you start doesn’t define where you finish. It’s about turning setbacks into fuel. It’s about building people, not just players.

Through KRA UK, Solo continues to push that message forward. Whether it’s running masterclasses, competing at elite level, or building relationships with organisations like the Fiji Rugby Union, his mission remains the same, to open doors that were once closed.

His story is still being written. But one thing is already clear: Solo isn’t just building a rugby academy. He’s building a legacy.

Follow KRA UK on Instagram for more updates; Instagram

item.title: Fiji, Australia boost economic relations
item.description: NEW business partnerships, investment opportunities and stronger economic ties between Fiji and Australia will be at the centre of discussions today as hundreds of business leaders gather in Suva. Fiji-Australia Business, to be held at the Grand Pacific Hotel in Suva, is themed “Strategy for a shifting landscape” and will focus on issues affecting businesses and the wider regional economy.
item.content:encoded:
NEW business partnerships, investment opportunities and stronger economic ties between Fiji and Australia will be at the centre of discussions today as hundreds of business leaders gather in Suva.

Fiji-Australia Business, to be held at the Grand Pacific Hotel in Suva, is themed “Strategy for a shifting landscape” and will focus on issues affecting businesses and the wider regional economy.

Fiji-Australia Business Council president Himen Chandra said the forum would bring together business, government and industry leaders to discuss emerging opportunities and challenges facing the region.

“Under the theme ‘Strategy for a shifting landscape,’ the forum will provide businesses with the strategic insights, connections, and opportunities needed to succeed in an evolving regional economy,” Mr Chandra said.

The two-day program includes discussions on the macroeconomic and industrial outlook, the Vuvale Partnership, multilateral engagement, workforce trends and standards, trade and investment, energy transition, the Brisbane 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games, and connectivity, destination branding and tourism.

The program also includes a strategic dialogue on the Vuvale Union, a session examining energy transition amid a fuel crisis, and discussions on opportunities linked to Brisbane 2032.

Among the speakers and panellists listed for the forum are Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka, Deputy Prime Minister Manoa Kamikamica, Australian High Commissioner Peter Roberts, Reserve Bank of Fiji Governor Arif Ali, Investment Fiji CEO Kamal Chetty and Fiji Airways CEO Paul Scurrah.

Other participants include Tourism Fiji CEO Dr Paresh Pant, Energy Fiji Ltd chairman Rokoseru Nabalarua, Fiji Development Bank CEO and Investment Fiji chairman Filimone Waqabaca, and Brisbane 2032 Organising Committee chief sport officer Christopher McConnell.

Representatives from organisations including the Asian Development Bank, World Bank Group, Austrade, Pacific Trade Invest Australia, Fiji National Provident Fund, Standards Australia and the Pacific Australia Skills initiative are also listed among the forum participants.

The program identifies the sessions as covering the macro and industrial dialogue, the Vuvale Union strategic briefing dialogue, a multilateral fireside chat, workforce and business trends, trade and investment, energy transition, Olympic opportunities and tourism and connectivity.

Mr Chandra said the forum would also look at the longstanding Fiji-Australia relationship and areas where new opportunities could emerge.

“From the enduring strength of the Vuvale Partnership to new frontiers in trade, investment, tourism, and sports (Brisbane 2032), the Forum will spark fresh conversations, forge meaningful connections, and inspire new opportunities for growth and collaboration.”

He said the 2026 forum would feature speakers, discussions and networking opportunities aimed at connecting business, government and industry representatives.
